fields.Back: At the sending host each layer adds its own header to the data (payload) received from the layer above: message M -> segment (Ht|M) -> datagram (Hn|Ht|M) -> frame (Hl|Hn|Ht|M).

fields.Text: Encapsulation: transport adds header {{c1::Ht}} to make a segment; network adds {{c2::Hn}} to make a datagram; link adds {{c3::Hl}} to make a frame.

fields.Front: What two kinds of fields does a packet have at each layer?
fields.Back: Header fields (added by that layer) and a payload field (typically the packet from the layer above).

fields.Front: Which layers does a link-layer switch implement, and which header does it examine?
fields.Back: Physical and link layers (layers 1-2); it examines the link header Hl and never looks at IP addresses.

fields.Front: Which layers does a router implement, and which header does it use to forward?
fields.Back: Physical, link and network layers (layers 1-3); it examines the network header Hn (destination IP address) to forward, and replaces the link header Hl for the outgoing link.

fields.Text: A switch implements {{c1::2}} layers (physical, link); a router implements {{c2::3}} layers (physical, link, network); a host implements all {{c3::5}} layers.

fields.Front: Which headers does a router change and which does it leave untouched?
fields.Back: It replaces the link-layer header Hl on each hop; the network header Hn, transport header Ht and message M pass through unchanged (aside from small IP field updates like TTL).

The reverse process at the destination: link layer removes Hl and passes the datagram up, network removes Hn and passes the segment up, transport removes Ht and delivers the message M to the application.
